nameStory: Autumn coralroot gets its name from two key features: it blooms in fall when most orchids are long done flowering, and its underground root system looks remarkably like branching coral. The coral-like roots are actually specialized structures that help this unusual orchid connect with soil fungi for survival.
description: Autumn coralroot is a leafless orchid that pops up from the forest floor like a slender, yellowish-brown stem topped with tiny purplish flowers. Growing 4-16 inches tall, this mysterious plant has no green parts at all and relies entirely on underground fungi partnerships to survive. It's one of New England's most unusual wildflowers, appearing ghost-like in late summer and fall woodlands with clusters of small, often barely-opening flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Leafless yellowish-brown to purplish stem rising directly from soil, often swollen or bulbous at the base, giving it an asparagus-like appearance when emerging

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny reddish-purple flowers with white lips spotted purple, arranged in a loose spike; many flowers remain closed (cleistogamous) and never fully open

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Completely absent - no green leaves whatsoever, only small brownish scales wrapped around the stem base

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Entire plant ranges from pale yellow to deep brown or purplish-brown, never green, giving it a dried or ghost-like appearance

habitat: Found in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly favoring areas with deep leaf litter and well-developed soil fungal networks. Look for it in mature woodlands with maples, oaks, and beeches, often on gentle slopes or in protected valleys where organic matter accumulates.

seasonality.spring: Completely absent above ground - the plant remains dormant as coral-like roots underground.
seasonality.summer: May begin emerging in late summer as yellowish-brown shoots pushing through leaf litter, but easily overlooked.
seasonality.fall: Prime season for finding autumn coralroot - stems fully developed with flowers blooming from August through October, standing out against fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the distinctive coral-like root system hidden in soil until next fall.

funFact: Autumn coralroot is essentially a plant vampire - it has no chlorophyll and can't make its own food, so it steals all its nutrients by parasitizing fungi in the soil through its coral-shaped roots!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other coralroot orchids, but autumn coralroot blooms much later (fall vs. spring/early summer) and has smaller, often closed flowers. Remember: 'autumn' coralroot blooms in autumn, while spotted and northern coralroots bloom in spring and early summer.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize this strange-looking plant is actually an orchid - it lacks the showy flowers we typically associate with the orchid family. The scientific name 'Corallorhiza' literally means 'coral root' in Greek, referring to the distinctive underground structure.
compareHints: Autumn coralroot is much smaller and more delicate than spotted coralroot, with tiny flowers that often don't open fully, and it blooms in fall rather than summer. Northern coralroot is also smaller but blooms in spring and has yellowish flowers. Autumn coralroot's late blooming period and frequently closed flowers make it the most distinctive of New England's coralroots.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern coralroot is much paler and blooms earlier than spotted coralroot, which has obvious purple spots and reddish coloring.
Spotted coralroot is much showier than its coralroot cousins, with larger flowers that actually open fully to display their distinctive spots.
